info.name: Chess Platform — Phase 1
info.description:
REST API for the chess platform, through Phase 1 (auth + gameplay).

## Run order
Folders are numbered. Run 1 before 2, and 3 or 4 after 1. Or hit **Run collection** to execute everything with assertions.

## Usernames are randomised
`whiteUsername` and `blackUsername` are seeded with a random suffix in the collection pre-request script, so re-running does not collide with accounts from the previous run. No teardown needed.

## The refresh cookie
It is set `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict`. Postman's cookie jar will not reliably replay a `Secure` cookie over plain HTTP, so the auth requests parse it out of `Set-Cookie` into a collection variable and send it back as an explicit `Cookie` header. A browser does this for you; Postman needs the help.

## Requires
`docker compose -f ops/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d` and the app running on `{{baseUrl}}`.

request.description: /me rather than /users/{id}: identity comes from the token, so there is no path parameter to tamper with and IDOR is unrepresentable.
Single-use. The response carries a DIFFERENT refresh cookie; the old one is now spent and presenting it again is treated as theft.

// will not reliably replay a Secure cookie over plain HTTP, so capture it here and

pm.test('a new refresh token was issued', () => pm.expect(pm.collectionVariables.get('whiteRefresh')).to.not.eql(old));

request.description: The unique constraint is what guarantees this, not the pre-check.
Minimum 12 chars, no composition rules. Length dominates entropy.
Binding to a DTO rather than the entity means `rating` cannot be set by the client.

Must be byte-identical to the wrong-password response, or login becomes a user-enumeration oracle. The server also hashes a dummy value so the TIMING matches — compare the two response times in Postman.
Structurally valid JWT, wrong signature. The decoder pins HS256 so the algorithm cannot be chosen by the attacker.

Presenting an already-rotated token cannot happen legitimately, so it is proof the lineage leaked. The WHOLE family is revoked — run the next request to confirm the current token died too. See ADR-013.

item.name: …and the current token is dead too → 401

request.description: This is the assertion that matters. Revoking only the presented token would leave the attacker's freshly-minted one working.

exec: pm.test('family revoked, not just the reused token', () => pm.response.to.have.status(401));

item.name: 3 · Play a game (scholar's mate)

request.description: playAs is pinned to WHITE for a deterministic run. Omit it in real use and colours are drawn at random — White scores ~54%, so always letting the challenger pick would be a way to farm rating.

exec: pm.test('starts active at ply 0', () => { pm.expect(b.status).to.eql('ACTIVE'); pm.expect(b.ply).to.eql(0); });

request.description: Full state + move log + legal moves. This is the polling fallback when the WebSocket is down, and the shape GAME_SNAPSHOT will carry in Phase 2.
Scholar's mate. White delivered it, so White wins — the mover is whoever was to move BEFORE the move, not after.

item.description: Run this folder top to bottom. It plays a complete game and verifies the result is attributed correctly.

request.description: 422, not 400. The request parsed perfectly; it is the position that refuses it. The client should resync its board, not change its serialisation.
Uses a FIXED clientMoveId so the next request is a genuine retry.

item.name: Idempotent move — retry returns the SAME result

request.description: Same key, same answer — and the move is applied once. Note expectedPly is still 0 and it succeeds anyway: the idempotency check runs BEFORE the stale check, because a retry is not a stale client.

exec: pm.test('ply did not advance twice', () => pm.expect(b.ply).to.eql(1));

request.description: Black missed white's move and is playing against a board it cannot see. Reject and resync rather than apply a move to a position the player never saw.
